claim: A change that changes nothing still bumps the revision, logs a Change, records an undo step that does nothing, and clears redo.
evidence:
text.rs:336-375: apply() records every op. undo.rs:182: record() runs `self.redo.clear()`.

Scratch crate, on "abc": insert(1,"x"), then insert(2,""), then replace(0..1,"a").
- rev goes from 0 to 3, with 3 log entries.
- undo 0 = Ok(0..1) and undo 1 = Ok(2..2) leave the text "axbc".
- Only undo 2 removes x.

Then insert(3,"d"), undo, delete(0..0) and redo gives Err(NothingToUndo): redo is lost.

Emacs records nothing for an empty deletion, and Vim's u after a no-op undoes the previous change. V3 produces such changes: `d0` at column 0, `~` on a digit, `gU` on uppercase, and `r` with the same character.
recommendation: Fix now. It's two lines, and V3 will hit it.

verifier.reasoning:
Partly confirmed. The mechanics reproduce in my scratch crate:
- insert(1,"x"), insert(2,"") and replace(0..1,"a") take the revision to 3 with 3 log entries;
- undo 0 = Ok(0..1) and undo 1 = Ok(2..2) both leave "axbc", and undo 2 removes the x;
- after insert, undo, then delete(0..0), redo gives Err(NothingToUndo).

But the "text replaced by itself" half is wrong against the oracle. I ran the user's own Evil in batch (verify-text-and-keys/evil/noop.el), doing x first, then the no-op, then u:
- `d0` at column 0 and `i<Esc>` record nothing: u undoes the x.
- `ra` on an a, `~` on 1, `gUiw` on FOO and `sa` on an a each record a step: u undoes the no-op and the x stays.

Emacs records casify-region and delete+insert pairs even when the text doesn't change, and Vim's `r` saves undo too. The proposed `retain(byte_slice != s)` would make `u` after `ra` undo the previous change, a deviation from Evil.

Only empty changes (empty range and empty text) are a defect: `d0` at column 0, an empty `c` motion, `p` with an empty register. That is narrower than the claimed major, and contained.

K10b's "a rewrite with the same bytes leaves no undo step" must then compare the bytes itself, which revert already has to do.

claim: The change log's order within a transaction, and the presence of undo and redo changes in it, are undocumented. A dot-repeat recorder that concatenates inserted text gets two inserts at one position reversed.
evidence:
text.rs:370 applies a transaction's changes from the last position to the first. Scratch: tx.insert(2,"A").insert(8,"B") logs rev 1 at 8, then rev 2 at 2.

With `insert(p,"(").insert(p,")")` (an auto-pair), the log holds ")" and then "(", although the text reads "()".

Contract §9, die-vim primitive 8, makes dot-repeat read edits_since. Undo and redo changes are logged with origin User and silent false (text.rs:393-404), and no test reads them (TEST-1, mutants E and F).

LOG_CAP is a const (text.rs:19), though A8 recommended a configurable cap.
recommendation: Doc now; die-vim's V4 recorder relies on it.

verifier.reasoning:
Scratch results:
- tx.insert(2,"A").insert(8,"B") logs rev 1 at 8, then rev 2 at 2.
- On "xy", insert(1,"(").insert(1,")") gives "x()y", but logs ")" (rev 1) and then "(" (rev 2). Concatenating the logged text gives ")(".
- Replaying the log in order, each change in the coordinates left by the one before, does reproduce the text. That is exactly the fact the rustdoc must state.

Other evidence:

- text.rs:393-404 logs undo and redo changes with Origin::User and silent false.
- Mutants E and F survive every test (my run).
- A8 (s4-core-api.md:146-148) recommended "per change, with the cap configurable", but LOG_CAP is a const (text.rs:19).

The proposed rustdoc matches the code: None when rev > rev(), or when the oldest logged revision is past rev + 1.

claim: add_marker accepts a position inside a character, where decorate refuses one. set_sticky ignores a dead id. point() panics past the end, where line_of clamps.
evidence:
Scratch: TextBuf::new("中x").add_marker(1, Left) gives a marker at 1, with is_boundary false. decorate returns BadRange for the same position (text.rs:569-576).

set_sticky (text.rs:602-606) returns () for a dead id, though C4 says a dead id is an error the type makes the caller handle.

point(3) on a 2-byte text panics with "Byte index out of bounds" (text.rs:289-295), while line_of (text.rs:280) clamps.
proposed_fix:
- `pub fn add_marker(&mut self, pos: usize, g: Gravity) -> Result<MarkerId>`: BadRange off a character boundary; still clamps to len().
- `pub fn set_sticky(&mut self, id: DecorationId, start: Gravity, end: Gravity) -> Option<()>`.
- point clamps like line_of, with rustdoc "/// The line and byte column of `b`, clamped to the end."
recommendation: Change the return types before extensions use markers.

verifier.better_fix:
The reviewer's three changes, plus:
```rust
/// Remove a marker; its last position, or None if `id` was already dead.
pub fn remove_marker(&mut self, id: MarkerId) -> Option<usize>
```
In the Gravity docs (DOCS-1), say "strictly inside replaced text": a position at the replaced range's start stays at the start, and one at its old end goes to the replacement's end, whatever its gravity (map_pos, text.rs:195-207).

claim: Text inserted at a cursor pushes that cursor forward in every window. Emacs leaves other windows' points before the new text.
evidence:
text.rs:438-442 maps every window's anchor and head with Gravity::Right.

Scratch: two windows with cursors at 1 in "abc", then a silent Extension insert of "XYZ" at 1, moves both cursors to 4.

Emacs's window points are markers that stay before insertions; comint follows output only via insert-before-markers. Vim's other windows keep their line and column.
proposed_fix: Map the acting window's head with Right, and every other head and every anchor with Left. Contract §9 Cursors sentence: "Text inserted at a cursor goes after the acting window's cursor and before every other window's, as Emacs's window points do."
recommendation: Adopt. The focused window still follows text streamed at its cursor.

verifier.reasoning:
- Scratch: two windows with cursors at 1 in "abc", then a silent Extension insert of "XYZ" at 1, moves both cursors to 4.
- map_all maps every window's anchor and head with Gravity::Right (text.rs:438-442).
- Emacs's non-selected window points are markers that stay before an insertion.
- For callbacks, actor = cur_window = focused (ctx.rs:1130). Under the proposal, the focused window follows a stream at its cursor and others don't.

The proposed "every anchor with Left" breaks the acting window's collapsed cursor. After typing at a cursor (anchor == head), the anchor stays and the head moves, so Selection::cursor becomes a selection over the inserted text.
verifier.decision_view: Adopt, with the acting window keeping Right for both ends. Another window's cursor stays where you left it, as in Emacs and Vim. An extension that wants a window to follow its output can set that window's cursor, as comint does.

claim: Two group behaviours are undocumented and untested: an explicit undo group that's never ended swallows every later command into one step, and undo or redo silently ends an open group.
evidence:
Scratch: begin_undo_group, then three commands each inserting a character, with no end. One undo removes all three ("abc" becomes "").

undo.rs:355: commit() sets depth to 0, so `u` inside an insert session ends it, and die-vim's later end_undo_group does nothing. Mutant C survives every test.

text.rs:466-473 rustdoc says neither.
recommendation: Doc now.

verifier.reasoning:
Scratch results:
- begin_undo_group, then three commands each inserting a character, with no end: one undo empties the buffer ("abc" becomes "").
- begin, a, b, then undo, gives "". Then c, d and end_undo_group: undo gives "c", and undo again gives "". So undo ended the group, and the later end did nothing.

The code agrees: History::commit sets depth = 0 (undo.rs:355), and end() returns early at depth 0 (undo.rs:279-282). The rustdoc at text.rs:466-473 says neither. Mutant C survives both suites (my run).

The proposed rustdoc matches the code:
- begin joins a group from the same command (undo.rs:267-275);
- groups nest by depth;
- undo and redo end the group.
It omits that undo_boundary still splits an open group into new steps (text.rs:474-476).
verifier.better_fix: Use the reviewer's rustdoc, adding after its second sentence: "`undo_boundary` still ends the current step early; the group stays open, as a new step."

claim: printable() returns the OS text even with Ctrl held, and winit's text for Ctrl chords is a control character. If R4 copies it, `<char>` matches Ctrl chords and insert state or the prompt types control characters. The `text` rustdoc's example also contradicts Option-as-Alt.
evidence:
S1 real run (spikes/s1-renderer/results/interactive-keys.json, 2026-11-03): winit's text is "\u0001" for C-a, "\u001b" for C-[, "\u0007" for C-g, "\u0000" for C-Space and "\r" for C-Return.

keys.rs:143 returns `text` before checking mods. Scratch: KeyEvent{key: Char('a'), ctrl, text: Some("\u{1}")}.printable() == Some("\u{1}").

Ghostty's ghostty_key_event_set_utf8 doc (die-term-sys bindings.rs:4893): "Do not pass C0 control characters ... pass NULL instead".

keys.rs:72 gives the example "é" from Option-e e, but keys.rs:49 says "DIE treats both Option keys as Alt", and S1's matrix tests "M-e (dead key on US/AU)" as Alt-e.

committed("") gives key Char(' ') with printable Some("").
recommendation: Fix before R4 maps events.

claim: Committed text of more than one code point comes back from notation as several keys. A recorded `r❤️`, `f👍🏽` or `f🇦🇺` replays as the first code point, followed by stray keys.
evidence:
keys.rs:321 writes committed text one character at a time. Scratch: committed("👍🏽") gives notation "👍🏽", and parse_keys gives 2 keys.

tests/notation.rs:206-213 asserts only the concatenated text: "Committed text comes back as one key per character". In normal state, the trailing U+FE0F or U+1F1FA is an unbound key.
proposed_fix:
In keys.rs typed(), merge runs of unmodified literal characters by grapheme cluster (unicode-segmentation, already a dependency). A cluster of more than one char becomes one `KeyEvent::committed(cluster)`.

In committed_text_round_trips, generate single-cluster texts (emoji with modifiers, flags, ZWJ sequences) and assert that `back.len()` is the number of clusters and each key's printable() is its cluster.
recommendation: Fix with V4.

verifier.reasoning:
Scratch, committed text through key_notation and parse_keys:
- "👍🏽", "🇦🇺" and "❤\u{fe0f}" each come back as 2 keys, for example [Char('👍'), Char('🏽')];
- "e\u{301}" comes back as 2 keys;
- "é" comes back as 1 key.

keys.rs:321 writes committed text one character at a time. tests/notation.rs:205-213 compares only the concatenated text.

Merging grapheme clusters in typed() is the right fix, but two details are missing:
- CR LF is a single extended grapheme cluster, so control characters must be excluded from the merge.
- notation_round_trips (notation.rs:198-203) asserts `back == evs` for random key presses. A generator that can produce two adjacent plain characters forming one cluster (a letter then a combining mark, or two regional indicators) would then fail.
verifier.better_fix:
In typed(): merge runs of unmodified `Key::Char` chords that come from literal characters (not `<lt>`, `<Space>`, `<Bar>` or `<Bslash>`) by extended grapheme cluster. Turn each cluster of more than one char that contains no control character into one `KeyEvent::committed(cluster)`.

In notation_round_trips, keep key_press from emitting combining marks, ZWJ, variation selectors or regional indicators.

In committed_text_round_trips, add single-cluster texts (skin-tone emoji, flags, ZWJ families, e plus U+0301). Assert that back.len() equals the cluster count and that each key's printable() is its cluster.

claim: In your GUI Emacs and in Vim, C-[ is Escape, C-i is Tab and C-m is Enter. In DIE they're separate keys, so C-[ doesn't leave insert state.
evidence:
Scratch: parse_pats("<C-[>") != parse_pats("<Esc>"), and parse_pats("<C-i>") != parse_pats("<Tab>").

S1's run: C-[ arrives as logical "[" with Ctrl.

dispatch (ctx.rs) would report "<C-[> is undefined" in insert state.

Kitty's protocol tells these keys apart, so the raw event must stay distinct for passthrough.
recommendation: Fold in chord(), which matches both references.

verifier.reasoning:
Scratch: parse_pats("<C-[>"), ("<C-i>") and ("<C-m>") each differ from <Esc>, <Tab> and <CR>.

die-vim's Insert keymap binds only `<char>` and `<Esc>` (die-vim/src/lib.rs:87-88), so C-[ is unbound there. With winit's text copied in, C-[ would even match `<char>` and type ESC (KEYS-1). S1 records C-[ as logical "[" with Ctrl and text \u001b.

GUI Emacs turns C-[, C-i and C-m into ESC, TAB and RET, and Vim does the same, so folding matches both references.

The proposed fold() arms don't check Shift. Ctrl-Shift-I would fold to Key::Tab with shift still set, which is `<S-Tab>`.
verifier.decision_view: Fold in chord(). It matches both of the user's references, and the raw event stays distinct for kitty passthrough. The cost is that `<C-i>` can't be bound apart from Tab, which neither Vim nor GUI Emacs allows either.

claim: Notation accepts three spellings that can't mean what they say: `<C-S-2>` binds a chord no key produces, `<S-Space>` is plain Space, and an unclosed `<C-a` binds four keys silently.
evidence:
Scratch: parse_pats("<C-S-2>") = Chord{Char('2'), ctrl}. keys.rs:286-292 uppercases only letters, then fold() drops Shift. The OS sends Ctrl-Shift-2 as Char('@'), since Shift is already applied (keys.rs:9), so the binding never fires; it should be written `<C-@>`.

parse_pats("<S-Space>") == parse_pats("<Space>").

parse_keys("<C-a") gives 4 keys. Contract §7:149 calls "modifiers followed by something that isn't a key" a startup error.
proposed_fix:
In bracket(): when has_mods and there's no closing `>`, return Err(format!("unclosed <{}", String::from_iter(&c[1..]))).

In chord(): return Result, with Err("write the shifted character, as in <C-@>, not <C-S-2>") when Shift is held with a Char that isn't an ASCII letter or a space.

In fold(): keep Shift on Key::Char(' ').
recommendation: Fix in K5's dispatch work.

verifier.reasoning:
Scratch results:
- parse_pats("<C-S-2>") = Chord{Char('2'), ctrl}, with Shift dropped, while the OS sends Ctrl-Shift-2 as '@'. S1 shows that logical keys come with Shift applied (C-S-a gives 'A').
- parse_pats("<S-Space>") == parse_pats("<Space>"); <S-1> gives plain '1'.
- parse_keys("<C-a") gives 4 keys, and "<C-x" gives '<','C','-','x'. Meanwhile <C-X-a> is an error.

The proposed fix is wrong in one part: keeping Shift on Space in fold(). Shift-Space typed while Shift is still held would then stop matching a `<Space>` binding, such as a Space leader, and DIE has no Emacs-style fallback that retries without Shift.

The unclosed-bracket error is fine: "<C-" stays literal (bracket() needs i + 2 < len), and no fixture uses an unclosed modifier.
verifier.better_fix:
In bracket(): when has_mods and there's no closing `>`, return `Err(format!("unclosed <{}", String::from_iter(&c[1..])))`.

In chord(): return Result. When Shift is written with any Key::Char that isn't an ASCII letter, Space included, return Err: "write the shifted character, as in <C-@>, not <C-S-2>", or for Space, "Shift doesn't change Space: write <Space>". Leave fold() as it is.

```rust
pub num_lock: bool,
```
```rust

Unidentified,
```
Doc on `unshifted`: "With `key`, this gives the terminal's consumed modifiers: Shift is consumed when `key`'s character differs from this one; Alt never is, since Option is Alt."

claim: 175 public items in scope have no rustdoc, including the units that matter most. K15 adds docs only after phase 1 has built on them.
proposed_fix:
Add `#![warn(missing_docs)]` to text.rs, text/search.rs, keys.rs, keymap.rs and layout.rs now. Key texts:
- Point: /// A position as a line and a column, both from 0. `col` counts bytes from the line's start (tree-sitter's convention).
- Gravity: /// Where a position goes when text is inserted exactly at it: `Left` stays before the new text, `Right` moves after it. Inside replaced text, `Left` goes to the replacement's start and `Right` to its end.
- Selection: /// A window's selection. `anchor` and `head` are byte offsets on cursor positions; `head` is the cursor. `Line` covers the lines from anchor's to head's; `Block`, the display columns between theirs on those lines.
- line_count: /// Lines as ropey counts them: text ending in a newline has an empty last line, so "a\n" has 2.
- Settings.max_width: /// The text area's width in cells; the gutter is outside it.
- Settings.tab_width: /// Cells per tab stop, counted from the display line's start; 0 counts as 1.
- Stop: /// `vcol` counts cells from the display line's start; `row` and `col` place it for the width the line was laid out at.
recommendation: Turn the lint on now, not at K15.

claim: In your fundamental-mode, Evil's * and # treat `_` as a non-word character, so `*` on foo matches inside foo_bar. Rust's `\<`, `\>` and `\b` count `_` as a word character, and Pattern has no way to say otherwise.
evidence:
Evil probe (probe/star.el, your ~/.emacs.d/lisp/evil, fundamental-mode as your .rs files open):
- `*` on the last foo of `x foo_bar foo` lands at 2, inside foo_bar;
- `*` from 0 in `foo foobar foo_bar` lands at 11, skipping foobar.

Evil's pattern is `\<foo\>` (evil-search.el:296-299).

Pattern::new takes only ignore_case (search.rs:25). Rust regex has no look-around. K8's search highlight takes the same Pattern, so filtering in die-vim alone would leave highlights and `n` disagreeing.
proposed_fix:
```rust
/// A literal pattern for `*` and `#`: `text` matches only where the characters on either side aren't word characters by `is_word` (Evil's in fundamental-mode: alphanumerics, not `_`). Rust's `\b` can't say this, since its word characters include `_`.
pub fn word(text: &str, ignore_case: bool, is_word: fn(char) -> bool) -> Result<Pattern>
```
It compiles the escaped literal. search, matches and match_at skip a match whose neighbouring characters pass `is_word`; search goes on from the rejected match's start + 1.

The alternative is a deviations.json entry with a fixture.
recommendation: Follow Evil (D4) with Pattern::word, since V1's `w` already stops at `_`.

verifier.reasoning:
The user's Evil (verify-text-and-keys/evil/star.el, fundamental-mode):
- `*` from the last foo of `x foo_bar foo` lands at 2, inside foo_bar;
- `*` from 0 in `foo foobar foo_bar` lands at 11, skipping foobar and landing in foo_bar;
- `w` from 0 in `foo_bar baz` lands at 3, on the `_`.

Evil's word search builds `\<%s\>` from the word under point (evil-search.el:1062-1065 for the evil-search module; the isearch module is the same). That word is always made of word characters.

The core side:
- Pattern::new takes only ignore_case (search.rs:25), and the Regex is private.
- Rust's `\b`, `\<` and `\>`, Unicode or ASCII, all count `_` as a word character, and there's no look-around.
- Because die-vim's word under the cursor follows Evil (foo, inside foo_bar), a `\bfoo\b` pattern wouldn't even match the foo the cursor is on.

A filter in core is the only way to keep the search highlight and `n` agreeing.
verifier.better_fix:
As proposed, with two precise points:
- After rejecting a match, resume at the next character boundary after its start, not start + 1 byte.
- last_before (backward search, used by `#` and N) must also skip rejected matches and keep looking further left.
verifier.decision_view:
Follow Evil, with Pattern::word.
- V1's `w` already follows Evil (it stops at `_`), so `*` picks foo in foo_bar.
- Rust's boundaries would then fail to match the word the cursor is on, which is worse than either reference.
- A deviation would also need a fixture and would contradict D4's goal of finding what Evil's searches find.

claim: The wrap rule as written contradicts Emacs's visual-line-mode on whitespace at the row's end, and says nothing about several cases that two independent implementations would resolve differently.
evidence:
Contract line 256 says: "A row ends after the last space or tab that fits on it, the breaking space included, and the next row starts with the next word."

The evidence is tty Emacs 30.2 on a pty (probe/probe.el, out.json, out2.json). A tty window W+1 wide breaks as GUI Emacs does at W: tty Emacs keeps its last column for the continuation glyph, and the probe gives the gj fixture's starts [0,35,65] at 40. At W=10:
- (a) `aaaa bbbb  cccc` gives Emacs rows `aaaa ` and `bbbb  cccc`. The sentence breaks after the first space after bbbb, which fits.
- (b) `aaaa` plus 8 spaces plus `bbbb` gives `aaaa` and 6 spaces, then `  bbbb`. The sentence drops or leads those 2 spaces, unstated.
- (c) `aaaaaaaaaa bbbb` gives `aaaaaaaaaa`, then ` bbbb`. The sentence is undefined: no space fits, and the word isn't longer than a row.
- (d) `aa bbbbbbbbbbbb` gives `aa `, then `bbbbbbbbbb`, then `bb`. Whether a long word starts its own row is unstated.
- (e) 9 a's, a tab and `bb`: the tab is split, 1 cell on row 0 and 6 on row 1. `cc\tdd` on a second row puts dd at row col 6, so tab stops count from the line's start.
- (f) Hidden text without replacement joins words: `aaaa bb[hidden space]cccccc` breaks before bb. Emacs breaks inside display strings and before-strings at their spaces (EOB at col 7).
- (g) NBSP, U+200B, U+3000 and `-` never break. U+200B takes 1 column. Cluster width is unstated: unicode-width 0.2.2 gives 2 for 👍🏽, 👨‍👩‍👧 and 🇦🇺, and tty Emacs 4.

In code, layout.rs:398 sorts virtual text by DecorationId, which is the slot index and reused after removal, not the order added.
proposed_fix:
Replace contract line 256 with:

**Where soft wrap breaks.** As Emacs's `visual-line-mode` (`word-wrap` t) does. Layout places a display line's items left to right on rows `text_w` cells wide.
- *Items*, in display order: each grapheme cluster of visible buffer text, each grapheme of a Hide's replacement, and each grapheme of virtual text. Clusters (extended, unicode-segmentation) are segmented within each run of visible text between Hide boundaries and line ends, so a Hide boundary inside a cluster splits it. Hidden text without a replacement adds no items, so the text on each side joins into one word. Virtual text comes just before the item at its position, in the order it was added. Virtual text inside hidden text or inside a cluster isn't shown.
- *Widths*: a tab reaches the next multiple of `tab_width`, counted in cells from the display line's start, not the row's. A control character other than tab and newline is one cell, drawn as `?`. Any other item is `unicode-width` 0.2's width of the whole cluster (no `cjk`), and at least one cell.
- *Whitespace* is U+0020 and U+0009 only.
- *Break points*: before an item that isn't whitespace and directly follows a whitespace item, unless it's the first item on its row.
- *When an item doesn't fit* (its last cell would be past the row's last cell): if the row has a break point at or before it, the row ends just before the last one, and the next row starts there; the whitespace before it stays at this row's end. Otherwise the row ends before the item: a tab is split, its cells that fit ending this row and the rest starting the next; a wide character moves to the next row whole, leaving filler cells; anything else starts the next row.
- *Line ends*: the newline and the end of the buffer take no cell and never start a row (see WRAP-2).
- *Cursor positions*: each is drawn on its item's first cell. A row break adds none.
- With soft wrap off, a display line is one row.

Examples at 10 cells: `aaaa bbbb cccc` gives `aaaa bbbb |cccc`; `aaaa bbbbb cccc` gives `aaaa |bbbbb cccc`; `aaaa bbbb  cccc` gives `aaaa |bbbb  cccc`; `aaaaaaaaaa bbbb` gives `aaaaaaaaaa| bbbb`; `aa bbbbbbbbbbbb` gives `aa |bbbbbbbbbb|bb`.

The Evil oracle's tty Emacs keeps its last column for the continuation glyph and otherwise breaks this way, so a fixture W columns wide is checked at W − 1 text columns.
